Baby & Child

Wilms tumor in children: symptoms, tests and treatment

Updated: November 10, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A new lump in a child’s tummy needs prompt medical assessment, even when the child seems well. There are several possible causes, and a lump does not by itself mean cancer. Wilms tumor is one condition the specialist team may investigate. If it is diagnosed, the next steps depend on the tumor’s features and the child’s health, rather than its size alone.

What is Wilms tumor?

Wilms tumor, also called nephroblastoma, is the most common kidney cancer in children. It usually appears in early childhood, often before age five, although older children can be affected. Most children have a tumor in one kidney; a smaller group have tumors in both. The kidneys filter blood, balance fluid and make urine, so treatment planning considers kidney function as well as cancer control.

This cancer develops from cells related to early kidney development. It is different from a kidney that formed abnormally or contains developmental cysts. A scan showing a kidney mass does not establish its exact type: other childhood kidney tumors exist and can require different care. A pediatric cancer team brings together the scans, laboratory results and examination of tissue to clarify the diagnosis.

Symptoms that should be checked promptly

A painless swelling or lump in the abdomen may be the first thing a parent notices, sometimes while dressing or bathing a child. Some children have few other symptoms. Others develop abdominal pain, blood in the urine, fever, nausea, poor appetite, weight loss or constipation. High blood pressure may be found during an examination. These findings are reasons for assessment, not a home diagnostic checklist.

Contact a clinician promptly about a new abdominal lump, persistent unexplained swelling or visible blood in urine; do not wait for pain to develop. Explain any persistent changes in appetite, energy or bowel habits too. Breathing difficulty, collapse, blue or grey coloring or unusual difficulty waking needs emergency help. A suspected tumor should be assessed through the local urgent pediatric pathway rather than left until a routine checkup.

Causes and inherited risk: avoid blame

Changes in genes controlling cell growth are involved, but most children do not have an inherited family pattern. Often no single explanation can be found for why one child developed the tumor. It is not evidence that a parent caused the cancer. Differences in age or population statistics cannot diagnose or rule it out in an individual child.

Some conditions increase risk, including WAGR syndrome, Beckwith–Wiedemann spectrum and certain WT1-related disorders, such as Denys–Drash syndrome. Findings such as aniridia, where the iris is partly or completely absent, differences in urinary or genital development, or one side of the body growing larger may prompt genetics assessment. A single feature does not establish a syndrome. Share family history and earlier diagnoses; the genetics team can advise about relatives and any surveillance needed.

How the team investigates a kidney mass

The assessment starts with the child’s history and an examination, including blood pressure. Ultrasound is often the first abdominal scan. MRI or CT can show the mass, both kidneys, nearby structures and blood vessels in more detail. Chest imaging checks for possible spread to the lungs. The team chooses tests according to the clinical question rather than ordering every available scan.

Blood tests assess blood counts, kidney function and other aspects of health needed for safe treatment; urine is checked for blood and other abnormalities. These tests cannot confirm Wilms tumor by themselves. Tissue examination provides information that scans cannot. A bone-density test is not a routine diagnostic or staging test for Wilms tumor; additional investigations are selected when there is a specific reason.

Why a biopsy is not always the first step

A biopsy removes a sample for a pathologist to examine. Some children need one before treatment, especially when the diagnosis is uncertain. Others have tissue examined after the operation that removes the tumor. The safest sequence depends on the child’s age, imaging findings, whether one or both kidneys are involved and the treatment protocol.

In many North American Children’s Oncology Group approaches, a removable one-sided tumor is operated on first. SIOP approaches, used in many European centers, commonly start with chemotherapy to shrink a typical tumor before surgery. There are exceptions, including very young infants and complex presentations. Ask why your team recommends its sequence and whether a biopsy would change staging or treatment; neither sequence is a rule for every child.

Stage and tumor-cell features answer different questions

Stage describes the extent of disease. In broad terms, stage I is confined to the kidney and completely removed; stage II extends beyond the kidney but is completely removed. Stage III includes disease remaining in the abdomen, affected abdominal lymph nodes, or tumor rupture or spillage. Stage IV means spread to distant sites, often the lungs. These are simplified descriptions: the exact criteria differ between protocols and include surgical and laboratory findings.

Stage V means tumors are present in both kidneys at diagnosis; each side also needs assessment. It is not simply a label meaning “worse than stage IV.” Histology describes what the cells look like. Favorable histology and anaplasia help guide risk assessment; after chemotherapy, other patterns, including surviving blastemal cells, also matter. Stage, cell features, selected biological findings and treatment response are considered together, rather than calling all of these a single “grade.”

Surgery aims to remove cancer safely

An operation often removes the affected kidney and tumor, with nearby lymph-node samples to check the extent of disease. Removing a whole kidney is called nephrectomy. It does not automatically mean that the adrenal gland and every nearby organ must also be removed. The surgeon plans the operation around the tumor’s location, surrounding structures and the need to avoid spilling tumor cells.

Partial nephrectomy removes the tumor while leaving some kidney tissue. It is particularly important to consider when both kidneys are affected, when there is only one functioning kidney or in selected predisposition conditions. It is not suitable for every one-sided tumor. Ask which tissue the team expects to preserve, what could change the plan during surgery and how kidney function will be checked afterward.

Chemotherapy and radiotherapy have different roles

Most treatment plans combine surgery with chemotherapy, using medicines to treat cancer cells. Chemotherapy may shrink a tumor before surgery or address remaining cancer cells afterward. Selected very-low-risk cases can receive less treatment under a specialist protocol. The drugs, number of courses and timing depend on the risk assessment; a general article cannot supply a safe treatment schedule.

Radiotherapy uses carefully planned radiation to treat cancer in particular areas. Some children need it, while others do not. The decision considers spread, histology, surgical findings and response to chemotherapy. The team balances control of the cancer with effects on a growing body. A clinical trial may be offered when appropriate; ask about its purpose, the usual treatment alternative and the extra commitments before deciding.

When both kidneys are affected

Bilateral Wilms tumor needs coordinated cancer and kidney expertise. Chemotherapy commonly comes first, with repeat assessment to help plan surgery that removes cancer while preserving useful kidney tissue. The operations and treatment afterward may differ on each side. Having tumors in both kidneys does not automatically mean both kidneys will be removed.

If too little working kidney tissue remains, dialysis may be needed to remove waste and excess fluid. A kidney transplant is considered only when medically appropriate, taking cancer control and the child’s overall condition into account. Timing is not determined simply by reaching a certain age. Ask the team to explain the likely kidney-function outlook and the alternatives if the initial plan changes.

During treatment, know whom to call

Before going home, obtain the cancer team’s daytime and out-of-hours contact instructions. Chemotherapy can reduce infection-fighting white blood cells. Fever or suspected infection during treatment needs immediate contact with the team and may require emergency assessment. Follow the child’s own temperature threshold and measurement instructions; do not wait for a high fever if they are unwell, and do not wait until morning.

Check with the team before giving nonprescribed medicines, supplements or fever-reducing medicine, which can mask a temperature. Do not use rectal medicines or rectal temperature measurement during treatment unless the oncology team specifically directs otherwise. Report persistent vomiting, poor drinking, reduced urine, new pain or other changes promptly. Severe breathing problems, collapse or difficulty waking requires emergency services while the oncology team is informed.

Outlook, recovery and follow-up

Many children with Wilms tumor are successfully treated, particularly with favorable tumor features. The outlook still varies with stage, histology, biology, response and whether the cancer has returned. Ask for an explanation based on your child’s results rather than applying an overall survival figure to them. If treatment is not working as hoped or the cancer returns, the team reassesses the available options.

After treatment, follow-up looks for recurrence and monitors the remaining kidney tissue. Blood pressure, urine and kidney-function checks may be needed. Other monitoring depends on treatment exposures: for example, some chemotherapy or radiotherapy can affect heart health, growth or fertility later. Ask for a treatment summary and a personalized survivorship plan that can travel with the child into adult care.

Make the plan understandable for your family

At an appointment, ask which results are confirmed, which are still pending and what decision comes next. Useful questions include: What is the stage and risk group? Why this order of treatments? Is kidney-preserving surgery possible? Which symptoms mean we must call immediately? A written explanation can help when several professionals are involved or a second specialist opinion is being arranged.

Practical and emotional support belongs alongside medical treatment. Ask about help with travel, time away from work, meals, childcare and school or nursery contact. Play specialists, psychologists and social workers can help children and families cope with unfamiliar procedures and uncertainty. Support should fit the child’s age and preferences, including siblings’ questions and the family’s need for an interpreter.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Seek prompt assessment for a new abdominal lump or visible blood in urine; ask how the urgent referral will be arranged.

Request a clear explanation of the diagnosis, stage, risk group and reasons for the treatment sequence.

Keep the cancer team’s urgent-contact instructions and the long-term treatment summary accessible to relevant caregivers.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organize appointments, questions and instructions from the care team. It cannot diagnose a kidney mass, determine cancer stage or decide that an unwell child receiving treatment can wait.

When to seek help

During cancer treatment, fever or suspected infection needs immediate contact with the oncology team, following the child’s own plan. Severe breathing difficulty, collapse or difficulty waking needs emergency help. Do not change cancer treatment or give additional medicines without advice.

Evidence notes updated: November 10, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A new abdominal lump or visible blood in urine needs prompt assessment even if the child seems well.
  • Wilms tumor is usually not an inherited family cancer; associated conditions need individual genetics advice.
  • Stage, tissue findings and treatment response guide care, and the sequence of treatment varies by protocol.
  • Most plans combine treatments; bilateral disease requires particular attention to preserving kidney function.
  • Keep immediate-contact instructions during treatment and a personalized follow-up plan afterward.

Frequently asked questions

What symptoms can Wilms tumor cause?

A painless abdominal swelling or lump may be the first sign. Blood in urine, pain, fever, nausea, poor appetite or constipation can also occur, while some children otherwise seem well. These symptoms have other causes, but a new lump or visible blood in urine should be checked promptly.

What causes it, and is it inherited?

Gene changes affecting cell growth are involved, but most cases have no inherited family pattern and no single identifiable cause. Certain genetic conditions increase risk. The diagnosis does not show that a parent caused the cancer; family history and associated findings guide genetics advice.

How is Wilms tumor diagnosed?

The team combines examination, blood pressure, blood and urine tests, and imaging of the kidneys and other relevant areas. A pathologist examines tissue, obtained by biopsy in selected cases or during surgery. Neither a blood test nor a scan alone provides every part of the diagnosis.

Can Wilms tumor be treated?

Yes. Many children are successfully treated. Surgery and chemotherapy are central to most plans, with radiotherapy for selected children. The child’s tumor features and response determine the plan and outlook; surgery alone is not the only possible treatment.

Does stage V always mean the worst outlook?

No. Stage V identifies tumors in both kidneys at diagnosis, rather than a simple step beyond distant spread. The team assesses both sides, histology and response, and tries to preserve kidney tissue where safe.

Why might another child have chemotherapy before surgery?

Different established protocols use different sequences, and individual findings can change the order. Some commonly begin with surgery for a removable one-sided tumor; others use chemotherapy first. Ask the team why its approach fits your child instead of comparing treatment order alone.

Will my child definitely need dialysis?

No. Many children retain enough kidney function after treatment. Dialysis is used when kidney function is insufficient, not simply because Wilms tumor is present. Bilateral disease requires careful planning, and transplantation is considered individually if needed.

When should we call during cancer treatment?

Contact the oncology team immediately for fever according to the child’s plan or suspected infection, and whenever they become unexpectedly unwell. Do not wait overnight or for a higher temperature. Severe breathing difficulty, collapse or unusual difficulty waking requires emergency help.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
